title: Spot the biased sample
subtitle: Evaluating statistical claims: Observational studies and experiments  · 3 official questions

sections.heading: Where this sits for you
body: **3 of the official questions in Evaluating statistical claims: Observational studies and experiments  are this one** — 1 Easy, 0 Medium, 2 Hard.
It is top-heavy: most versions are Hard, so it only earns study time once your target actually requires that tier.

sections.heading: How to spot it
body: You are looking at this pattern when:
- The sample was chosen by convenience (whoever was at one location), by self-selection (viewers or visitors who chose to respond), or from a subgroup that obviously has a stake in the answer.
- The choices argue about sample size, about whether the sample should be 'more' or 'less' of some group, or about whether the method is flawed or biased.

sections.heading: The method
body: - 1) Compare the population the question wants to learn about with the group that was actually sampled.

- 2) If the sample was not randomly chosen from that whole population (it was self-selected, convenient or a special subgroup), choose the answer that calls it non-random or unrepresentative and possibly biased.
- 3) Rule out 'sample too small' unless the method was random and size really is the only issue.

sections.heading: What it is built to catch
body: You blame the sample size instead of how the sample was chosen.
Or you accept a fix that swaps one unrepresentative subgroup for another, such as sampling only the opposite group.
Or you treat a clear majority in a biased sample as proof about the whole population.

sections.heading: You are losing these
body: Before you choose, say out loud what the question is asking for — not what you solved for.
You blame the sample size instead of how the sample was chosen.
Or you accept a fix that swaps one unrepresentative subgroup for another, such as sampling only the opposite group.
